A systematic way to scan a Memory Match board

Use a repeatable four-by-four scan to remember symbol locations in the current seeded Memory Match layout.

By NoCharge·Reviewed by NoCharge·Published August 15, 2026·Updated November 24, 2026·2 min read
Try the detail in a live board.

Flip cards. Find pairs.

Play Memory MatchBrowse all Articles

Bottom line: Give each position a row-and-column name, then keep the same scan order. Memory Match’s current seeded board repeats after reset, so a consistent map helps you learn where each symbol is.

The board is a four-by-four grid with eight symbol pairs. The current source uses a fixed seeded shuffle rather than a new random arrangement on every reset. That makes the opening layout reproducible; it does not change the two-card rules.

Start with a fixed map

Number the spaces mentally from left to right and top to bottom, or use row and column names. “Triangle, row two, column three” is easier to act on than “I saw a shape somewhere in the middle.” You do not need to remember every card at once; keep short location notes in mind.

Use each attempt for a reason

The first card reveals a symbol. If its partner is already known, choose that remembered location second. Otherwise, reveal a new position and retain both pieces of information. A mismatch is still one move, but it can expand the map for the next attempt.

Sweep consistently

A left-to-right, top-to-bottom sweep helps you tell which positions you have already inspected. After a pair is matched, those cards become unavailable; continue with the remaining board and keep using row-and-column labels rather than counting a fixed number of keyboard presses.

Keep the goal modest

A scan does not guarantee a perfect run, and the visible move count is not a saved personal record. The current count resets with the board. Try one run with a fixed sweep, then use the current game page for controls or read how Memory Match counts moves.
